newsitem.title: MAURITANIA: Toxic algae threaten rare seals off Mauritania.
newsitem.headline: Toxic algae threaten rare seals off Mauritania.

text.p: More than 60 monk seals, one of the world's most endangered species, have been killed by toxic algae off Mauritania's Atlantic coast in the past 10 days, Spanish researchers said on Monday.

The scientists, working with the national oceanographic and fisheries research centre, said the seals had been poisoned by eating fish that had swallowed the algae. Their bodies had washed up near the port of Nouadhibou.
The seals were part of a colony previously estimated at 150, living off the Mauritanian coast. Ecologists say the species numbers no more than 350 worldwide.
So called because folds of skin around their necks recall monastic dress, they are among the last members of the seal family living in temperate waters in the northern hemisphere.
Two baby monk seals were rescued and are recovering in the centre's aquarium in Nouadhibou.

The algae grow quickly in the warmer waters of the Gulf Stream, and one ecologist said they were considering moving the seals from Cap Blanc into the Banc d'Arguin bay to the south where the algae would be less prevalent.
A baby monk seal who had apparently lost her parents in a storm was treated at the centre and released back into the sea in January 1996.
